newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Eurotunnel has votes for debt plan-source.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurotunnel has votes for debt plan-source.

text.p: Eurotunnel has sufficient shareholder votes to ensure approval of a crucial 70 billion franc ($11.7 billion) debt restructuring plan, a source at the Channel Tunnel operator said on Thursday.
Eurotunnel needs the approval of holders of two-thirds of the French shares and three-quarters of the British shares to pursue the deal struck in April with its leading bank lenders.
The source said the company had a "crushing majority" of votes, sufficient to clear both hurdles, at an extraordinary general meeting held in Paris.
Eurotunnel said votes for 272.3 million shares were present or represented at the meeting, or 29.62 percent of the total that would have been eligible.
It said executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle held proxies for 177.7 million votes representing 19.32 percent.

The debt deal would cut interest charges to 3.2 billion francs this year from 5.7 billion paid in 1996, giving Eurotunnel breathing room, but would cut shareholders' equity to 54.5 percent with the creditor banks taking 45.5 percent.
Christian Cambier of the Eurotunnel Shareholders' Association, who said before the meeting that his group would vote for the deal, holds proxies for 2.05 percent.
Shareholder rights activist Sophie l'Helias and FGIS, who will also vote in favour, have 0.80 percent.

Albert Jauffret of shareholder group Adacte, who said he would vote the 12 million shares for which he had proxies against the deal, had not signed the acceptances for the mandates given to him, Eurotunnel said.
Belgium's Tractebel and its Belga Manche unit will vote their 10 million shares in favour of the deal, Tractebel said.
The prospect for the deal's approval grew last week after the French and British governments said they would consider extending Eurotunnel's operating licence to 99 years from the current 65.
They also said if the debt deal was not approved, they would not be able to keep the banks from taking over Eurotunnel's operating licence -- a declaration that swayed l'Helias.
Others who had switched in favour of the deal include Bermuda-based Northern Cross Investments.

Ponsolle told the meeting Eurotunnel was on track for a better performance. He reiterated that it expected to show a loss of 2.72 billion francs this year, less than half the 1996 loss of 6.1 billion francs.
The improvement hinges on the debt plan being approved.
Ponsolle said he was "extremely confident" the group could reach the targets previously set to turn a profit in 2005 and pay a dividend the following year.

Eurotunnel has been hobbled from the outset by a construction bill of 10 billion pounds, nearly twice the original cost estimate for the 51-km sub-sea link, and lower-than-targetted revenue since service began in 1994.

The agreement struck with the banks in April followed more than a year of negotiations. Shareholders were due to vote on the plan at a meeting on June 24 that was cancelled when not enough shareholders attended to form a quorum.
